sections.title: 1. Streams, Sinks, and the Decorator Architecture
sections.description: Understand why network programming starts with file I/O, how data flows from sources to sinks, and how java.io composes capabilities via decorators.

blocks.title: Streams, Packages, and the Decorator Pattern
blocks.content:
In Java, **files and TCP sockets share the exact same I/O abstraction**: you read from an `InputStream` and write to an `OutputStream` regardless of whether the other end is an SSD or a remote host.

* **Pipeline roles:** **Source** (producer: file, socket, `System.in`) → **Stream** (sequential byte/char flow) → **Sink** (consumer: file, socket, `System.out`).

| Package | Role | Exam Relevance |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`java.io`** | Classic stream-based I/O (`InputStream`, `OutputStream`, `Reader`, `Writer`) | **Primary API** for files & TCP sockets |
| **`java.nio`** | Non-blocking channels/buffers | Only use **`java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets`** |
| **`java.util.stream`** | Functional collection pipelines (`.map()`, `.filter()`) | Unrelated concept (bridged via `BufferedReader.lines()`) |

### Two Hierarchies & Decorator Composition
| Operation | Binary Data (Raw Bytes) | Text Data (Characters + Encoding) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Read** | `InputStream` (abstract) | `Reader` (abstract) |
| **Write** | `OutputStream` (abstract) | `Writer` (abstract) |
| **Examples** | PNG, BMP, WAV, ZIP, `.class` | Source code, CSV, JSON, HTTP headers |

`java.io` uses the **Decorator Pattern**—wrapping an object inside another of the same interface to layer capabilities (buffering, charset decoding, data parsing):
* **Inside-out construction:** Innermost stream connects to the OS (`FileInputStream`, `socket.getInputStream()`); outer layers add buffering or character decoding.
* **Cascading `close()`:** Closing the outermost decorator automatically flushes and closes every wrapped inner stream.
* **Shortcut:** `new FileReader(path, charset)` is shorthand for `new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(path), charset)`.

blocks.title: The java.io Decorator Chain
blocks.caption: Text streams wrap binary streams: raw bytes flow from a file or socket, pass through a memory buffer, get decoded into UTF-16 characters by InputStreamReader, and are buffered for line-by-line reading.

sections.title: 2. Binary Data, Buffering, and Endianness
sections.description: Learn why InputStream.read() returns an int, how 8 KiB buffering eliminates millions of expensive syscalls, how block reads behave on networks, and why byte order matters.

blocks.title: Reading & Writing Bytes: The `int` vs `byte` Trap
blocks.content:
Processing binary data follows three steps: open a stream (`FileInputStream` / `FileOutputStream`), read/write bytes, and close the stream.

Three crucial details govern `InputStream.read()` and `OutputStream.write(int)`:

1. **`read()` returns `int`, not `byte`:**
   In Java, `byte` is **signed** (`-128` to `+127`). If `read()` returned a `byte`, there would be no spare value to signal End-of-Stream (EOF) because `-1` is already a valid byte (`0xFF`)! Instead, `read()` returns an `int` in the range **`0` to `255`** for a valid byte, or **`-1`** at EOF.
2. **`write(int)` keeps only the lowest 8 bits:**
   Calling `out.write(300)` does **not** write the integer `300`. Since `300 = 0x12C`, `write(int)` masks out everything above 8 bits (`300 & 0xFF`) and writes **`0x2C` (`44`, ASCII `,`)**.
3. **`read()` is blocking:**
   It pauses execution until at least 1 byte is available or the stream ends. On a local file this is instantaneous; on a network socket, `read()` may block for seconds or minutes waiting for the remote peer.

blocks.title: Byte-by-Byte Binary Read/Write Loop

annotations.note: Must be int, not byte! Storing read() in a byte would turn 0xFF (255) into -1 and prematurely stop the loop.
read() blocks until 1 byte arrives (returns 0..255) or EOF is reached (returns -1).
write(int) writes only the lowest 8 bits of b to the underlying sink.

blocks.title: Why Buffering Makes I/O 200x Faster (and Block Reads)
blocks.content:
Every unbuffered `read()` / `write()` triggers an **OS syscall** for a single byte—10 MiB byte-by-byte = ~10.5M syscalls (~12,800 ms on NVMe).

Wrapping with `BufferedInputStream` / `BufferedOutputStream` adds an **8 KiB (8,192-byte) RAM buffer**:
* **Read:** 1 syscall fetches 8 KiB; the next 8,191 `read()` calls hit RAM.
* **Write:** Accumulates in RAM until full (or `flush()`/`close()`), then 1 syscall.
* **Result:** 10 MiB drops from **~12,800 ms** to **~60 ms** (~200x faster).

### Block Reading (`read(byte[])`) — Even Faster
```java
byte[] buffer = new byte[8192];
int n;
while ((n = in.read(buffer)) != -1) {
  out.write(buffer, 0, n);
}
```
> [!WARNING]
> **Three Critical Exam Traps:**
> 1. **Short Reads:** `in.read(buffer)` returns *1 to `buffer.length`* bytes. Getting fewer than `buffer.length` mid-transfer on a socket is normal—**only `-1` means EOF**.
> 2. **Never call `out.write(buffer)`:** Always use `out.write(buffer, 0, n)`! Otherwise the final short read writes stale leftover bytes from the previous iteration (e.g., turning a 10,000-byte file into 16,384 bytes).
> 3. **Always `flush()` open network streams:** Buffered output stays in RAM until full or closed. On a persistent socket, forgetting `out.flush()` makes the remote peer hang forever.

blocks.title: Endianness: Network Byte Order vs. Little-Endian
blocks.content:
A single byte needs no ordering, but multi-byte integers (`short`, `int`, `long`) can be laid out in memory or on the wire in two ways:

* **Big-Endian (Most Significant Byte first):** `0x12345678` is stored as `0x12 0x34 0x56 0x78`. Used by **Internet protocols (IP, TCP, UDP — RFC 791 "network byte order")** and Java's `DataInputStream` / `DataOutputStream`.
* **Little-Endian (Least Significant Byte first):** `0x12345678` is stored as `0x78 0x56 0x34 0x12`. Used by x86/ARM CPUs, BMP images, WAV audio, and Protocol Buffers.

`InputStream` and `OutputStream` never interpret multi-byte numbers—they just move raw bytes. Reading a little-endian integer with a big-endian decoder produces a completely wrong number *silently*, with no exception thrown.

blocks.title: Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian for 0x12345678
blocks.caption: Big-Endian (network byte order) places the most significant byte (0x12) at the lowest address; Little-Endian places the least significant byte (0x78) first.

blocks.title: Practice: Byte Truncation & Endianness in Memory
blocks.instructions:
Complete `Main` using `ByteArrayOutputStream` and `ByteArrayInputStream` to:
1. Write `300` with `out.write(300)` and verify that reading it back yields `44` (`0x2C`).
2. Write `0x12345678` in **Big-Endian** order (4 bytes) using `DataOutputStream` (or bit shifts), then read the 4 raw bytes and reconstruct the `int` in Big-Endian.
hints: Remember that `byte` in Java is signed. Mask with `bytes[i] & 0xFF` before formatting as hex.
Use `String.format("%02X", bytes[i] & 0xFF)` inside a loop over `bytes`.

sections.title: 3. Text Data, Unicode, and UTF-8
sections.description: Discover why bytes are not characters, how mojibake happens, how UTF-8 encodes code points into 1-4 bytes, and why Java's String.length() lies about emojis.

blocks.title: Bytes Are Not Characters: ASCII, Code Pages, and Mojibake
blocks.content:
A byte is just 8 bits. A **character** is an interpretation of one or more bytes according to an agreed-upon **character encoding (charset)**. Files rarely store their encoding inside the file itself—both writer and reader must agree on it.

### What Goes Wrong When Encodings Disagree?
* **Mojibake (garbled text):** Writing `"élève"` in **UTF-8** (`C3 A9 6C C3 A8 76 65`) and reading it as **ISO-8859-1 / Windows-1252** produces **`Ã©lÃ¨ve`** because each 2-byte UTF-8 character is misinterpreted as two separate Latin-1 characters.
* **Irreversible Data Loss:** Writing `"élève"` in **US-ASCII** replaces any character outside 0–127 with `?` (`0x3F`), producing **`?l?ve`**—the original accents are destroyed forever.

### From 7-Bit ASCII to Code Pages
* **ASCII (1963):** 7 bits (`0`–`127`). Control chars `0`–`31` & `127` (including `LF = 10`, `CR = 13`), digits `'0' = 48 (0x30)`, uppercase `'A' = 65 (0x41)` to `'Z' = 90 (0x5A)`, lowercase `'a' = 97 (0x61)` (always uppercase + `32` / `0x20`). No accented letters.
* **8-Bit Code Pages (`128`–`255`):** Kept ASCII for `0`–`127` and assigned regional characters to `128`–`255`—e.g., **ISO-8859-1** (Latin-1), **ISO-8859-15** (adds `€`, `œ`, `Ÿ`), **Windows-1252** (adds `€`, curly quotes). Incompatible across regions and unable to represent Chinese/Japanese.

blocks.title: Unicode vs. UTF-8: Catalogue vs. Byte Encoding
blocks.content:
**Unicode is not an encoding.** Unicode is a universal catalogue assigning every character (over 150,000 assigned, out of `U+0000` to `U+10FFFF`) a numeric **code point**:
* `A` = `U+0041`, `é` = `U+00E9`, `€` = `U+20AC`, `😂` = `U+1F602`.
* `U+0000`–`U+FFFF` is the **Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP)** (most living scripts). Emojis and rare scripts live above `U+FFFF` and need up to 21 bits.

**UTFs (Unicode Transformation Formats)** define how code points map to bytes:

| Encoding | Bytes per Code Point | ASCII Compatible? | Primary Use |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **UTF-8** | 1 to 4 bytes | **Yes** | The Web, Linux, macOS, JSON, modern files |
| **UTF-16** | 2 or 4 bytes | No (`'A'` is `0x00 0x41`) | Java `String`, JavaScript, Windows internals |
| **UTF-32** | Always 4 bytes | No | Rare (fixed width, 4x memory overhead) |

### UTF-8 Variable-Length Bit Layout

| Code Point Range | Bytes | Bit Pattern (`x` = code point bits) | Example |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| `U+0000`–`U+007F` | 1 | `0xxxxxxx` | `'A'` (`U+0041`) → `41` |
| `U+0080`–`U+07FF` | 2 | `110xxxxx 10xxxxxx` | `'é'` (`U+00E9`) → `C3 A9` |
| `U+0800`–`U+FFFF` | 3 | `1110xxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` | `'€'` (`U+20AC`) → `E2 82 AC` |
| `U+10000`–`U+10FFFF` | 4 | `11110xxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx 10xxxxxx` | `'😂'` (`U+1F602`) → `F0 9F 98 82` |

**Worked Example (`€` = `U+20AC`):** `0x20AC` in binary is `0010 0000 1010 1100` (16 bits → 3-byte pattern). Filling the `x` slots left-to-right gives `11100010 10000010 10101100` = **`E2 82 AC`**. Notice how leading bits (`0`, `110`, `1110`, `11110`) vs continuation bytes (`10`) make UTF-8 self-synchronizing.

blocks.title: Java `char` vs. Code Points, Surrogate Pairs, and the UTF-8 BOM
blocks.content:
Inside Java, a `String` stores text in **UTF-16**. This has two major consequences:

1. **`char` is a 16-bit UTF-16 code unit, NOT a Unicode code point!**
   Code points above the BMP (like `😂` `U+1F602`) do not fit in 16 bits. UTF-16 splits them into a **surrogate pair** (`0xD83D 0xDE02`, i.e., `55357` and `56834`).
   * `"I😂DAI".length()` returns **`6`** (UTF-16 `char` units), not `5`!
   * `"I😂DAI".codePointCount(0, 6)` returns **`5`** (actual Unicode code points).
   * `"I😂DAI".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length` returns **`8`** (`4` ASCII bytes + `4` bytes for `😂`).
   * Note: Some emojis like the Swiss flag `🇨🇭` are *two* code points (8 UTF-8 bytes), and `é` can be decomposed as `e` + combining accent (`U+0065 U+0301`).

2. **The UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (`0xEF 0xBB 0xBF`):**
   Windows tools (Notepad, Excel "CSV UTF-8") often prepend the bytes **`EF BB BF`** (UTF-8 encoding of `U+FEFF`) to the start of a file. In UTF-8, byte order is irrelevant, so the BOM is useless—and **Java does not strip it automatically**! `reader.readLine()` returns `"\uFEFFname,age"`, so `header.startsWith("name")` evaluates to **`false`**.
   **Fix:** Before your read loop on a `BufferedReader`, peek at the first character:
   ```java
   reader.mark(1);
   if (reader.read() != '\uFEFF') {
     reader.reset();
   }
   ```

3. **Always specify the charset explicitly:**
   Even though Java 18+ defaults file APIs to UTF-8 (JEP 400), always pass `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly so your code is self-documenting and portable to older JVMs.

blocks.title: Practice: Counting `char`s, Code Points, and UTF-8 Bytes
blocks.instructions:
Run and complete `Main` to inspect `"I😂DAI"` and `"élève"`:
1. Print `length()` (UTF-16 units) vs `codePointCount(0, s.length())` vs UTF-8 byte count for `"I😂DAI"`.
2. Print the UTF-8 hex bytes of `"élève"` (using `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`).
blocks.expected_output:
I😂DAI -> chars: 6, codePoints: 5, utf8Bytes: 8
C3 A9 6C C3 A8 76 65
hints: Call `french.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)` to encode the String into UTF-8 bytes.
Format each byte with `String.format("%02X", b & 0xFF)`.

sections.title: 4. Reader/Writer Chains, Line Endings, and Try-with-Resources
sections.description: Build the canonical 3-layer text I/O chain, handle LF vs CRLF line endings portably, prevent resource leaks with try-with-resources, and choose the right java.io class every time.

blocks.title: The Reader/Writer Chain & Portable Line Endings
blocks.content:
Text I/O on files or network sockets is **always built on top of byte streams**. The canonical 3-layer chain mirrors on both reading and writing:

1. **Raw Byte Stream:** `FileInputStream` / `FileOutputStream` (or `socket.getInputStream()` / `socket.getOutputStream()`).
2. **Charset Bridge:** `InputStreamReader` / `OutputStreamWriter` with explicit `StandardCharsets.UTF_8`.
3. **Line/Block Buffer:** `BufferedReader` / `BufferedWriter`.

### Line Endings: LF (`\n`) vs. CRLF (`\r\n`)
| Environment | Convention | Bytes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Linux, macOS | **LF** | `\n` (`0x0A`) |
| Windows, HTTP, SMTP | **CRLF** | `\r\n` (`0x0D 0x0A`) |

* **`BufferedReader.readLine()`** accepts `\n`, `\r\n`, or lone `\r`, **strips** the line ending, and returns **`null`** at EOF. (Warning: never use `reader.ready()` to detect EOF—`ready()` only tells you if the next read won't block right now!)
* **When writing:** `readLine()` removed the line ending, so you must append one yourself. Define an explicit constant like `static final String EOL = "\n";` (or `"\r\n"` for network protocols like HTTP/SMTP) rather than calling `System.lineSeparator()` or `BufferedWriter.newLine()`, which silently change behavior depending on the host OS.

blocks.title: Canonical 3-Layer Text Chain with Explicit Charset & EOL

annotations.note: Explicit EOL constant ensures identical output on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
InputStreamReader bridges raw bytes to characters using an explicit Charset.
Loop until readLine() returns null (never use reader.ready() for EOF detection).
readLine() strips the original line ending, so we append EOL explicitly.

blocks.title: Errors, `AutoCloseable`, and `try`-with-Resources
blocks.content:
I/O fails routinely (missing files, permissions, full disks, dropped connections). Key exceptions:
* **`IOException` (Checked):** Parent of all I/O errors (`FileNotFoundException` is a subclass). The compiler forces you to catch or declare `throws IOException`.
* **`UnsupportedCharsetException` (Unchecked):** Thrown by `Charset.forName("BOGUS")`. Because it is unchecked, the compiler will not warn you—catch `IllegalArgumentException` (its parent) if the charset name comes from user input.

### Why `try`-with-Resources Beats `finally`
Open streams hold OS file descriptors (a scarce limit) and buffered writers hold unflushed data in RAM. Manual `close()` inside `try` leaks resources if an exception occurs mid-loop; manual `finally` blocks require nested `try-catch` for every `close()` call.

**`try`-with-resources** works on any class implementing **`AutoCloseable`** (all `InputStream`, `OutputStream`, `Reader`, `Writer`, and `Socket` classes):
* Resources declared in `try (...)` are closed **automatically** when the block exits—whether normally or via an exception.
* They are closed in **reverse order** of declaration (last opened, first closed).
* If opening the first resource throws (e.g., `FileNotFoundException` on the input file), the second resource (`writer`) is **never opened**, so no empty destination file is created!

blocks.title: Decision Table: Which Class for Which Job?
blocks.content:
| You need to… | Binary Data | Text Data |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Read / write a file** | `FileInputStream` / `FileOutputStream` | `FileReader` / `FileWriter` (with `Charset`) |
| **Turn bytes into chars & back** | — | `InputStreamReader` / `OutputStreamWriter` (with `Charset`) |
| **Work in memory** | `ByteArrayInputStream` / `ByteArrayOutputStream` | `StringReader` / `StringWriter` |
| **Go fast (always buffer!)** | `BufferedInputStream` / `BufferedOutputStream` | `BufferedReader` / `BufferedWriter` |
| **Read line by line** | — | `BufferedReader.readLine()` |

> [!CAUTION]
> **Common Java I/O Pitfalls to Avoid:**
> * **Do NOT use `PrintWriter`:** It silently swallows I/O errors (its methods never throw `IOException`; you'd have to remember `checkError()`). Use `BufferedWriter` instead.
> * **Do NOT omit the `Charset`:** Code without an explicit `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` works by luck on your machine and breaks elsewhere.
> * **Do NOT use `BufferedReader.ready()` for EOF:** Loop until `readLine() == null`.
> * **Do NOT use `write(buffer)` after `read(buffer)`:** Always `write(buffer, 0, n)`.

blocks.title: Practice: Strip UTF-8 BOM & Normalize CRLF to LF
blocks.instructions:
Given a raw UTF-8 byte array starting with a UTF-8 BOM (`0xEF 0xBB 0xBF`) and containing Windows CRLF (`\r\n`) line endings, use the 3-layer `BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(...))` chain inside `try`-with-resources to:
1. Skip the leading BOM (`\uFEFF`) if present (using `mark(1)` and `reset()`).
2. Read lines and write them to a `ByteArrayOutputStream` via `BufferedWriter` using `\n` line endings.
3. Print the resulting UTF-8 string and its byte length.
blocks.expected_output:
Starts with name: true
Output bytes: 16
hints: Call `reader.mark(1); if (reader.read() != '\uFEFF') { reader.reset(); }` before the `while` loop.
"name,age\nAda,36\n" is 9 + 7 = 16 bytes once the 3-byte BOM and 2 `\r` bytes are removed.

sections.title: 5. Exam Synthesis
sections.description: Connect character encoding boundaries, buffering flushes, and line-ending conventions to real TCP network programming.

blocks.title: Synthesis: Why Encoding Boundaries & Flushing Matter on Networks
blocks.prompt: Imagine you are building a TCP chat server in Java. Why must you: (1) explicitly specify `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` on `InputStreamReader`/`OutputStreamWriter`, (2) call `flush()` after sending each chat message through a `BufferedWriter`, and (3) use `"\r\n"` or `"\n"` explicitly rather than `System.lineSeparator()`?
self_check_criteria: Explained that without an explicit Charset, clients/servers on different OSes or older JVMs may decode bytes differently, causing mojibake.
Explained that BufferedWriter holds outgoing text in an 8 KiB RAM buffer; without flush() on an open socket, the message never leaves the sender until the buffer fills or closes.
Noted that System.lineSeparator() varies by OS (LF on Linux/macOS, CRLF on Windows), breaking network protocol expectations.
blocks.model_answer: 1. Encoding happens at the byte-to-character boundary. If the server and client do not explicitly agree on UTF-8, multi-byte characters like accents or emojis turn into mojibake on mismatched machines. 2. A BufferedWriter buffers writes in RAM to minimize syscalls; unlike a file that closes right away, a chat socket stays open, so without flush() the remote user waits indefinitely for data stuck in your buffer. 3. Network protocols mandate fixed line endings (e.g., CRLF in HTTP/SMTP), whereas System.lineSeparator() changes depending on whether the server runs on Windows or Linux.

sections.title: 6. Diagnostic Assessment & Spaced Repetition
sections.description: Test your mastery of Java I/O streams, buffering, endianness, UTF-8 bit layouts, BOMs, and resource management.

blocks.title: Why InputStream.read() Returns int
blocks.question: Why does `InputStream.read()` return an `int` instead of a `byte`?
options: Because Java's `byte` is signed (-128 to 127), so an `int` is needed to represent all 256 unsigned byte values (0–255) plus `-1` for end-of-stream.
Because `read()` automatically decodes UTF-16 characters, which require at least 16 bits.
Because CPU registers are 32-bit, so returning a `byte` would cause a compilation error on 64-bit JVMs.
Because `read()` returns the total number of bytes remaining in the file.
blocks.correct_answer: Because Java's `byte` is signed (-128 to 127), so an `int` is needed to represent all 256 unsigned byte values (0–255) plus `-1` for end-of-stream.
blocks.explanation:
Java has no unsigned `byte` type (`byte` ranges from `-128` to `127`). If `read()` returned `byte`, the valid byte `0xFF` would equal `-1`, making it indistinguishable from End-of-Stream (EOF). Returning `int` allows `0`–`255` for data and `-1` for EOF.

* UTF-16 decoding is the job of `Reader`, not `InputStream`.
* Java methods can freely return `byte` on any JVM.
* `read()` returns the byte value itself, whereas `read(byte[])` returns the count of bytes read.
hints: Consider the range of values a Java `byte` can hold (-128 to 127).
How would a program distinguish a valid `0xFF` byte from End-of-Stream if `read()` returned `byte`?

blocks.title: Predict Output: OutputStream.write(int)
blocks.explanation:
`OutputStream.write(int)` writes only the **lowest 8 bits** of the argument. Since `300 = 256 + 44` (`0x12C` in hex), discarding the upper bits leaves `0x2C` = `44`.

* `300` is wrong because a single `write(int)` call writes only 1 byte, not a 4-byte `int`.
* `255` would be clamping/saturation, which `OutputStream` does not do.
* `-1` is only returned at EOF, not after writing 1 byte.
hints: How many bytes does a single call to `OutputStream.write(int)` write?

blocks.title: Block Copy Bug: write(buffer) vs write(buffer, 0, n)
blocks.question: You copy a 10,000-byte file using an 8,192-byte `byte[] buffer` and write `out.write(buffer)` instead of `out.write(buffer, 0, n)`. What happens?
options: The output file is 16,384 bytes long, with 6,384 stale bytes from the first block appended at the end.
Java throws an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` on the second iteration.
The output file is truncated to 8,192 bytes.
The output file is 10,000 bytes long because `OutputStream` tracks `n` automatically.
blocks.correct_answer: The output file is 16,384 bytes long, with 6,384 stale bytes from the first block appended at the end.
blocks.explanation:
On iteration 1, `read(buffer)` fills all 8,192 bytes. On iteration 2, it reads the remaining `10,000 - 8,192 = 1,808` bytes into `buffer[0..1807]`, leaving `buffer[1808..8191]` untouched from iteration 1. Calling `out.write(buffer)` writes all 8,192 bytes anyway, yielding `8,192 + 8,192 = 16,384` bytes.

* No exception is thrown because `buffer` has length 8,192.
* `OutputStream` has no knowledge of `n` unless you pass `(buffer, 0, n)`.
hints: How many iterations does the loop run for 10,000 bytes with an 8,192-byte buffer?
What is inside `buffer[1808..8191]` after the second `read(buffer)` call?

blocks.title: Flushing on Open Network Streams
blocks.question: A client wraps a `Socket`'s `OutputStream` in a `BufferedWriter`, writes `"HELLO\r\n"`, and waits for the server's reply without closing the socket. Both programs hang forever. Why?
options: The message is still sitting in the 8 KiB RAM buffer because `flush()` was not called.
TCP sockets do not support `BufferedWriter`.
`"\r\n"` is not a valid line ending for `BufferedWriter`.
The client forgot to call `BufferedReader.ready()` before reading.
blocks.correct_answer: The message is still sitting in the 8 KiB RAM buffer because `flush()` was not called.
blocks.explanation:
Buffered streams accumulate data in memory until the 8 KiB buffer is full or `close()`/`flush()` is called. Because `"HELLO\r\n"` is only 7 bytes and the socket remains open, the bytes never leave the client's RAM—so the server's `readLine()` blocks forever waiting for data.

* `BufferedWriter` works great with sockets when flushed.
* `"\r\n"` is the standard line ending for text network protocols.
* `ready()` does not fix an un-sent message.
hints: When does a `BufferedWriter` normally send its data to the OS?
In a request-response protocol, you cannot call `close()` before reading the reply. What method forces buffered data out?

blocks.title: Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian Representation
blocks.question: How is the 32-bit integer `0x12345678` stored in **Little-Endian** byte order (e.g., in a BMP or WAV file)?
blocks.explanation:
Little-Endian stores the **Least Significant Byte (LSB)** first (`0x78`), followed by `0x56`, `0x34`, and finally the Most Significant Byte (`0x12`).

* `0x12 0x34 0x56 0x78` is Big-Endian (network byte order).
* `0x87 0x65 0x43 0x21` mistakenly reverses the nibbles *inside* each byte (endianness orders bytes, not bits/nibbles).
* `0x56 0x78 0x12 0x34` swaps 16-bit halves rather than 8-bit bytes.
hints: Little-Endian means 'least significant byte first'.
Endianness reverses the order of whole bytes (pairs of hex digits), not individual hex digits.

blocks.title: Diagnosing Mojibake vs. Data Loss
blocks.question: You open a text file and see `Ã©lÃ¨ve` instead of `élève`. What happened?
options: The file was written in UTF-8 and decoded as ISO-8859-1 (or Windows-1252).
The file was written in US-ASCII and decoded as UTF-8.
The file was written in ISO-8859-1 and decoded as US-ASCII.
The file starts with a UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (BOM).
blocks.correct_answer: The file was written in UTF-8 and decoded as ISO-8859-1 (or Windows-1252).
blocks.explanation:
In UTF-8, `é` (`U+00E9`) is encoded as two bytes: `C3 A9`. When an ISO-8859-1 / Windows-1252 decoder reads those bytes, it interprets `0xC3` as `Ã` and `0xA9` as `©`, turning `élève` into `Ã©lÃ¨ve`.

* Writing in US-ASCII would have replaced `é` and `è` with `?` (`?l?ve`).
* A UTF-8 BOM adds `\uFEFF` at the very start of the file, not `Ã©` in place of `é`.
hints: Notice that each accented letter turned into TWO characters (`Ã©` and `Ã¨`).
Which encoding turns `é` into 2 bytes (`C3 A9`), and which 1-byte encoding turns `C3` and `A9` into `Ã` and `©`?

blocks.title: UTF-8 Byte Length Calculation
blocks.question: How many bytes does the string `"Aé€😂"` occupy when encoded in UTF-8? (Enter a single integer)
blocks.explanation:
Sum the UTF-8 byte lengths of each code point:
* `'A'` (`U+0041`, ASCII): **1 byte**
* `'é'` (`U+00E9`, 2-byte range `U+0080`–`U+07FF`): **2 bytes**
* `'€'` (`U+20AC`, 3-byte range `U+0800`–`U+FFFF`): **3 bytes**
* `'😂'` (`U+1F602`, 4-byte range `U+10000`–`U+10FFFF`): **4 bytes**
Total: `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10` bytes.
hints: Check each character's code point range in the UTF-8 table: ASCII (1), accented Latin (2), Euro/CJK (3), Emoji (4).
Add the four byte counts together.

blocks.title: Predict Output: String.length() vs. codePointCount()
blocks.explanation:
`String.length()` counts UTF-16 `char` units. `'H'` (1) + `'i'` (1) + `'😂'` (`U+1F602`, stored as a 2-`char` surrogate pair `0xD83D 0xDE02`) = **4 `char` units**. `codePointCount()` counts actual Unicode code points = **3**.

* `3 3` ignores surrogate pairs.
* `6 3` confuses UTF-8 byte length (`1 + 1 + 4 = 6`) with UTF-16 `char` count.
hints: Remember that Java `String` uses UTF-16 internally.
An emoji above `U+FFFF` requires a surrogate pair of two `char`s.

blocks.title: The Invisible CSV Header Bug
blocks.question: You read the first line of a UTF-8 CSV exported from Excel with `BufferedReader.readLine()`. It prints as `name,age`, yet `line.startsWith("name")` returns `false`. Why?
options: Excel prepended a UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (`0xEF 0xBB 0xBF` / `\uFEFF`), which Java does not strip automatically.
`readLine()` includes the trailing `\r\n` at the end of the line.
UTF-8 encodes `'n'` as two bytes at the start of a file.
`BufferedReader` pads the start of every file with a space.
blocks.correct_answer: Excel prepended a UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (`0xEF 0xBB 0xBF` / `\uFEFF`), which Java does not strip automatically.
blocks.explanation:
Windows tools like Excel often write the 3-byte UTF-8 BOM (`EF BB BF`) at the start of a file. Java decodes it into the invisible character `\uFEFF`, making the first line `"\uFEFFname,age"` so `startsWith("name")` is `false`.

* `readLine()` strips line endings, and even if it didn't, `startsWith` checks the *beginning* of the string.
hints: What invisible character (`U+FEFF`) do Windows tools like Notepad and Excel write at byte 0 of UTF-8 files?
Does Java's `InputStreamReader` automatically remove `U+FEFF`?

blocks.title: Guarantees of try-with-resources
blocks.question: Which statements about Java's `try`-with-resources are **true**? (Select all that apply)
options: Resources declared in `try (...)` are closed automatically even if an exception is thrown inside the `try` block.
Multiple resources are closed in reverse order of their declaration (last opened, first closed).
If opening the first resource throws `FileNotFoundException`, the second resource is never opened.
It only works for classes in `java.io`, not for network `Socket`s or custom classes.
correct_answer: Resources declared in `try (...)` are closed automatically even if an exception is thrown inside the `try` block.
Multiple resources are closed in reverse order of their declaration (last opened, first closed).
If opening the first resource throws `FileNotFoundException`, the second resource is never opened.
blocks.explanation: `try`-with-resources works with **any** class implementing `AutoCloseable` (including `Socket`, `ServerSocket`, database connections, and custom classes)—not just `java.io`. It guarantees automatic closing even on exceptions, closes resources in reverse declaration order, and halts resource initialization immediately if an earlier resource fails to open.
hints: What interface must a class implement to be used in `try`-with-resources?
When the first resource in `try (...)` fails to open, is the second resource ever initialized?

blocks.title: Identifying Common Java I/O Pitfalls
blocks.question: Which of the following practices are **bugs or anti-patterns** in Java I/O? (Select all that apply)
options: Using `while (reader.ready())` to detect the end of a file or stream.
Using `PrintWriter` instead of `BufferedWriter` for network or file output.
Using `System.lineSeparator()` when writing an HTTP or SMTP message.
Passing `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly to `InputStreamReader`.
correct_answer: Using `while (reader.ready())` to detect the end of a file or stream.
Using `PrintWriter` instead of `BufferedWriter` for network or file output.
Using `System.lineSeparator()` when writing an HTTP or SMTP message.
blocks.explanation:
* `ready()` only checks whether the next read will block right now—it is **not** an EOF check (`readLine() != null` is).
* `PrintWriter` silently swallows `IOException`s.
* `System.lineSeparator()` depends on the host OS, whereas HTTP/SMTP require `"\r\n"` everywhere.
* Passing `StandardCharsets.UTF_8` explicitly is a **best practice**, not a pitfall!
hints: Three of these cause silent bugs or protocol failures; one is a recommended best practice.
Check which method only tests non-blocking availability rather than EOF, and which writer swallows IOExceptions.

blocks.title: UTF-8 Byte Count by Script
blocks.front: How many bytes per code point does UTF-8 use for: ASCII, accented Latin/Cyrillic/Arabic, CJK (`€`), and Emojis?
blocks.back:
* **1 byte (`0xxxxxxx`):** ASCII (`U+0000`–`U+007F`)
* **2 bytes (`110xxxxx 10xxxxxx`):** Accented Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic
* **3 bytes (`1110xxxx ...`):** CJK, `€` (`U+20AC`)
* **4 bytes (`11110xxx ...`):** Emojis (`U+10000`–`U+10FFFF`)
blocks.hint: 1, 2, 3, or 4 bytes depending on code point range.

blocks.title: UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (BOM)
blocks.front: What are the 3 bytes of a UTF-8 BOM, what code point is it, and how do you skip it in `BufferedReader`?

blocks.title: Line Endings: LF vs. CRLF
blocks.front: What line endings do Linux/macOS, Windows, and HTTP/SMTP use, and why avoid `System.lineSeparator()`?
blocks.back:
* **Linux/macOS:** LF (`\n`, `0x0A`)
* **Windows & HTTP/SMTP:** CRLF (`\r\n`, `0x0D 0x0A`)

Avoid `System.lineSeparator()` because it changes output across OSes; use an explicit `EOL` constant.
blocks.hint: Network protocols require predictable bytes regardless of server OS.
